summary: Sets out the charter of the main IETF discussion mailing list, the general forum for Internet technology topics that have no dedicated list. It allows wide latitude in topics but also describes the kinds of posts that are unsuitable. It replaces the earlier charter in RFC 3005. It is a Best Current Practice document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9245 explains what belongs on the IETF discussion list and how the list is moderated. It also explains where to appeal a moderation decision and replaces the earlier charter in RFC 3005.

subtitle: The charter for the IETF's general discussion mailing list: its purpose, boundaries, and moderation process.

tldr.problem: The IETF needs a general place to discuss Internet topics that do not have a dedicated mailing list, with clear guidance about suitable posts and moderation.
tldr.mechanism: The charter defines the list's scope, describes inappropriate posts, and gives moderators authority to restrict posting when content shows a pattern of abuse, with an appeal path to the IETF Chair and IESG.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9245 replaces RFC 3005, updates RFC 3683, and has itself been updated by RFC 9945.

today: RFC 9245 is a Best Current Practice updated by RFC 9945. It obsoletes RFC 3005 and updates RFC 3683.

sections.title: Purpose of the Discussion List
sections.content:
The IETF discussion list supports the development and specification of Internet technology. It is a general forum for technical, procedural, operational, and other topics that do not have a dedicated list. The IETF Note Well and its conduct and anti-harassment policies apply to discussion on this list.

This charter replaces RFC 3005, reflecting other lists that now cover some topics and clarifying moderation procedures. It also updates the list of inappropriate postings copied into RFC 3683.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the IETF discussion list for Internet topics that do not have a more suitable mailing list. The IETF's conduct policies apply there as they do on its other mailing lists.

sections.title: Suitable and Unsuitable Posts
sections.content:
The list is for discussions that do not fit an existing working-group, area, or other established list. If another list is a better fit, participants should identify it and move the discussion there. When no list exists, requesting a dedicated list may be preferable.

Suitable posts include early discussion of technical issues that may become IETF work, practical questions about IETF meetings, announcements of events sponsored or endorsed by the IETF, IRTF, IAB, or Internet Society, and general discussion of IETF direction or standards policy when no better list exists.

Advertising and unsolicited bulk email are inappropriate. So are topics unrelated to IETF policy, meetings, activities, or technical matters; uncivil commentary; and announcements of events not sponsored or endorsed by the named organizations. Last Call discussions and IETF administrative policy discussions have dedicated lists.
sections.plainLanguage: Before posting, check whether a more focused list exists. The charter permits relevant IETF discussion and excludes advertising, unrelated subjects, uncivil commentary, and announcements from organizations outside its stated scope.

sections.title: How the Charter Changed
sections.content:
The RFC explains why it obsoletes RFC 3005. Some topics once discussed on the general list now have dedicated lists. The new text also refers to applicable conduct policies and clarifies how moderators operate and how their decisions may be appealed.

Because RFC 3683 copied the earlier list of inappropriate postings, RFC 9245 updates that part of RFC 3683 with the list in Section 2 of the new charter.
sections.plainLanguage: The revised charter recognizes that some topics have moved to their own lists. It also replaces the earlier list of inappropriate posts and clarifies how moderation and appeals work.

sections.title: Moderators and Appeals
sections.content:
The IETF Chair appoints moderators. They may restrict a person's posting or posting to an email thread when inappropriate content forms a pattern of abuse. They are encouraged to consider a person's overall posting history and whether a post is typical or an exception.

The moderator team independently defines, publishes, and carries out its procedures. The Chair appoints the team but should not manage its day-to-day work. Moderators should contact the Chair for conflict resolution. A moderator who joins the IESG or IAB steps down because those bodies are part of the appeal path.

A moderator decision may be appealed to the IETF Chair under RFC 2026. A decision by the Chair may then be appealed to the IESG as a whole.
sections.plainLanguage: Moderators may restrict posting when inappropriate behavior becomes a pattern. A person can appeal a moderator's decision to the IETF Chair, then appeal the Chair's decision to the IESG.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the usual security considerations for protocol documents do not apply. It identifies a risk that moderation could be used to suppress opinions someone dislikes, and says the appeal process counteracts that risk.

The document requests no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC identifies possible misuse of moderation to suppress opinions. It points to the appeal process as a way to challenge a decision.

viz.caption: APPEALS PATH FOR A MODERATION DECISION

messages.label: Appeal
messages.note: A moderator decision may be appealed to the IETF Chair.

messages.label: Further appeal
messages.note: A Chair decision may be appealed to the IESG as a whole.
